```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

rm(list = ls())
if (rstudioapi::isAvailable()) {
  setwd(dirname(rstudioapi::getActiveDocumentContext()$path))
}

out_dir <- "../../output/5_inference_final"
topic_path <- "../../input/topics/topic_labels.csv"
cov_dir <- "../../input/covariates"

fmt <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
f1 <- function(x) ifelse(x < 0.1, sprintf("%.3f", x), sprintf("%.2f", x))
or3 <- function(m, l, u) sprintf("%s (%s-%s)", f1(m), f1(l), f1(u))
mech_names <- c(ER = "Emotional Reactions", IP = "Interpretations", EX = "Explorations")
llm_names <- c(gemini = "Gemini", openai = "OpenAI", grok = "Grok")
llm_cols <- c(Gemini = "#0072B2", OpenAI = "#D55E00", Grok = "#009E73")
CREDIBLE_PD <- 0.975
EXPLORATORY_BELOW <- 0.05
is_cred <- function(pd, lcl, ucl) pd > CREDIBLE_PD & (lcl > 1 | ucl < 1)

# --- data size and raw rates (same weighting as the models) ---------------
cells <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "qc_filter_and_balance.csv"))
n_threads <- n_distinct(cells$post_id)
n_synth <- sum(cells$original_n)
n_real <- sum(distinct(cells, post_id, real_count)$real_count)

raw <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "inference_results.csv")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(response_post) & response_post != "")
rc <- raw %>% filter(source == "real") %>% count(post_id, name = "real_count")
raw <- raw %>%
  left_join(rc, by = "post_id") %>% mutate(real_count = coalesce(real_count, 0L)) %>%
  group_by(post_id, model, method) %>% mutate(cell_n = n()) %>% ungroup() %>%
  mutate(w = ifelse(source == "real", 1, pmin(1, real_count / cell_n))) %>% filter(w > 0)
raw <- raw %>% mutate(n_words = lengths(strsplit(as.character(response_post), "\\s+")))
words_med <- raw %>% mutate(who = ifelse(source == "real", "real", model)) %>%
  group_by(who) %>% summarise(med = median(n_words), avg = mean(n_words), .groups = "drop")
wmed <- function(w) words_med$med[words_med$who == w]
wavg <- function(w) words_med$avg[words_med$who == w]
raw_rates <- raw %>%
  mutate(who = ifelse(source == "real", "Real clinicians", paste("AI:", llm_names[model]))) %>%
  group_by(who) %>%
  summarise(ER = weighted.mean(ER_label >= 1, w), IP = weighted.mean(IP_label >= 1, w),
            EX = weighted.mean(EX_label >= 1, w), .groups = "drop")
raw_all <- raw %>% group_by(source) %>%
  summarise(ER = weighted.mean(ER_label >= 1, w), IP = weighted.mean(IP_label >= 1, w),
            EX = weighted.mean(EX_label >= 1, w), .groups = "drop")
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x)
pct1 <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x)

# --- topics ---------------------------------------------------------------
topics <- read.csv(topic_path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
lookup <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v2_topic_lookup.csv"))
n_topics <- nrow(lookup)
n_threads_in <- sum(lookup$n_threads)
n_expl <- sum(lookup$exploratory)
n_cancer <- sum(tolower(topics$cancer_relevant) == "true", na.rm = TRUE)
n_cancer_na <- sum(!tolower(topics$cancer_relevant) %in% c("true", "false"))
sev_raw <- read.csv(file.path(cov_dir, "severity.csv"))
n_sev_na <- sum(is.na(sev_raw$severity_score))

# --- results --------------------------------------------------------------
conv <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v2_topic_convergence.csv"))
sdp <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v2_topic_sd_summary.csv"))
sdl <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v2_llm_sd_summary.csv"))
canc <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v2_topic_cancer_moderation.csv"))
covs <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v2_covariate_effects.csv"))
sevm <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v2_severity_moderation.csv"))
tp <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v2_topic_gap_by_topic.csv"))
tl <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v2_topic_by_llm.csv"))
dl <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v2_llm_differences_by_topic.csv"))

avg <- tp %>% filter(is.na(topic))
bt <- tp %>% filter(!is.na(topic)) %>% mutate(credible = is_cred(shift_pd, shift_lcl, shift_ucl))
avg_llm <- tl %>% filter(is.na(topic)) %>% mutate(who_n = llm_names[who])
btl <- tl %>% filter(!is.na(topic)) %>% mutate(credible = is_cred(shift_pd, shift_lcl, shift_ucl), who_n = llm_names[who])
dl <- dl %>% mutate(credible = is_cred(shift_ratio_pd, shift_ratio_lcl, shift_ratio_ucl))

# --- strategy analyses (3j_strategy_models.R) and subsampling check -------
v3conv <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v3_convergence.csv"))
v3sens_conv <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v3_IP_sensitivity_convergence.csv"))
v3sens <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v3_IP_sensitivity_no_topic_intercept.csv"))
ge <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v3_group_effects.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(credible = is_cred(pd, lcl, ucl))
len_eff <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v3_length_effect.csv"))
v3sd <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v3_topic_by_group_sd.csv"))
v3dev <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v3_topic_by_group_deviations.csv"))
sub_cmp <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v3sub1_comparison_group_effects.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
sub_top <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v3sub1_topic_shift_comparison.csv"))
sub_conv <- bind_rows(lapply(c("ER", "IP", "EX"), function(m)
  read.csv(file.path(out_dir, sprintf("v3sub1_%s_convergence.csv", m)))))
strat_names <- c(dg = "DG", sag = "SAG", sagii = "SAGII")
model_order <- c("gemini", "openai", "grok")
star <- function(txt, cred) paste0(txt, ifelse(cred, " *", ""))
gx <- function(spec, level, who, mech, contrast = "") {
  r <- ge[ge$spec == spec & ge$level == level & ge$who == who & ge$mechanism == mech & ge$contrast == contrast, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(r) == 1); r
}
gx_txt <- function(...) { r <- gx(...); or3(r$or, r$lcl, r$ucl) }
n_within <- sum(ge$spec == "length adjusted" & ge$level == "strategy_within_model")
n_within_cred <- sum(ge$credible[ge$spec == "length adjusted" & ge$level == "strategy_within_model"])
n_across <- sum(ge$spec == "length adjusted" & ge$level == "strategy_across_models")
n_across_cred <- sum(ge$credible[ge$spec == "length adjusted" & ge$level == "strategy_across_models"])
per_doubling <- function(m) len_eff$or[len_eff$mechanism == m]^log(2)
sub_len <- sub_cmp %>% filter(spec == "length adjusted", level == "group")
sub_max_pct <- 100 * (exp(max(abs(sub_len$lratio))) - 1)
sub_flip_n <- sum(sub_cmp$cred_w != sub_cmp$cred_s)

gap_of <- function(df, m, w = NULL) { r <- df[df$mechanism == m & (if (is.null(w)) TRUE else df$who == w), ]; stopifnot(nrow(r) == 1); r }
sev_cred <- sevm %>% mutate(credible = is_cred(sev_pd, sev_lcl, sev_ucl))
```

# In short

Earlier analyses showed that AI-written replies to patient questions show
less empathy than real clinician replies. This report asks **when** the gap is
larger or smaller. We tested five things that might change it: the medical
topic of the question, *which* AI model wrote the reply, which *prompting
strategy* the model was given, how severe the patient's problem is, and
whether cancer is involved.

- **The gap depends strongly on the kind of empathy.** On average, AI replies
  are much less likely than real ones to react emotionally (odds ratio
  `r f1(gap_of(avg, "ER")$gap_or)`) or to explore the patient's experience
  (`r f1(gap_of(avg, "EX")$gap_or)`). For interpretations the average is closer to
  parity (`r f1(gap_of(avg, "IP")$gap_or)`).
- **The three AI models differ a lot, and for interpretations they differ in
  direction.** Grok's replies show interpretation *more* often than real
  clinicians' (odds ratio `r f1(gap_of(avg_llm, "IP", "grok")$gap_or)`); Gemini's
  (`r f1(gap_of(avg_llm, "IP", "gemini")$gap_or)`) and OpenAI's
  (`r f1(gap_of(avg_llm, "IP", "openai")$gap_or)`) show it less often.
  Averaging over models hides this.
- **Topic matters, but modestly and mostly for explorations.** The gap varies
  across the `r n_topics` topics for all three kinds of empathy
  (`r sum(bt$credible)` topic-level differences are credible), but the pattern
  is topic-specific rather than one topic standing out everywhere.
  Dermatology is the clearest case: AI explores relatively *more* there, and
  reacts emotionally relatively *less*.
- **Topic effects are mostly shared across models and prompting
  strategies.** Only `r sum(dl$credible)` of the model-versus-model comparisons
  within a topic are credible, both for explorations. Allowing the topic
  effect to differ by model or by strategy adds almost nothing, except for
  explorations, where it differs by model (Section \@ref(res-strat)).
- **Severity matters for interpretations.** The more severe the problem, the
  more AI replies catch up with real ones on interpretations, for all three
  models and under every prompting strategy. For emotional reactions this
  holds for Gemini and OpenAI only; for explorations we find no effect.
- **Cancer-related questions shift the gap in opposite directions for
  interpretations (AI relatively better) and explorations (AI relatively
  worse).**
- **Prompting strategy matters much less than the model, but not nothing.**
  Averaged over the three models, the strategies differ clearly only for
  emotional reactions (DG falls furthest behind real replies; ratios to SAG and SAGII
  `r gx_txt("length adjusted", "strategy_across_models", "all", "ER", "dg - sag")` and
  `r gx_txt("length adjusted", "strategy_across_models", "all", "ER", "dg - sagii")`);
  for interpretations there is only a borderline difference, and for explorations none.
  Within single models, `r n_within_cred` of `r n_within` strategy comparisons are
  credible, and the pattern is model-specific (for example, OpenAI's DG replies
  trail real ones most in emotional reactions), so there is no single "best"
  strategy (Section \@ref(res-strat)).
- **Reply length changes the interpretation story.** Longer replies are far
  more likely to be classified as showing interpretation (the odds roughly
  `r f1(per_doubling("IP"))` times for each doubling of length). OpenAI's replies are
  more than twice as long as real ones (median `r wmed("openai")` vs.
  `r wmed("real")` words). Without length adjustment OpenAI therefore appears to show
  *more* interpretation than real clinicians (gap
  `r gx_txt("no length adjustment", "model", "openai", "IP")`); at equal length it shows less
  (`r gx_txt("length adjusted", "model", "openai", "IP")`). Both versions are reported
  side by side (Section \@ref(res-len)).
- **The results do not depend on how we handle the surplus of AI replies.**
  Randomly thinning AI replies, instead of weighting them, changes estimated
  odds ratios by at most `r sprintf("%.0f%%", sub_max_pct)` and does not change the pattern of
  findings; only borderline comparisons change their credibility status (Section \@ref(res-sub)).

Everything here describes what automatic classifiers detect in text, and the
topic labels are themselves machine-made and imperfect (see
Section \@ref(caveats)).

# The study in plain terms

## The data

Each item is a patient question posted on Reddit's r/AskDocs. For each of the
`r fmt(n_threads)` threads we have the replies of real, verified clinicians
(`r fmt(n_real)` replies) and replies written by three AI models (Gemini,
OpenAI, Grok) given the same post, each under three prompting strategies
(`r fmt(n_synth)` AI replies in total). We keep the nine model-by-strategy
combinations apart in the models. The main results are reported per AI model;
Section \@ref(res-strat) examines the prompting strategies themselves.

## What was measured

Three classifiers, trained on the EPITOME framework of empathy in text-based
support, rated every reply on three kinds of empathy:

- **Emotional reaction (ER):** expressing warmth, concern or sympathy
  ("I'm sorry you're dealing with this").
- **Interpretation (IP):** showing an understanding of what the patient is
  feeling or experiencing ("it sounds like this has been worrying you").
- **Exploration (EX):** probing the patient's experience with follow-up
  questions ("how long has this been going on?").

Each is rated none, weak or strong. Replies with any empathy are
uncommon, so we ask a yes/no question: *does this reply show this kind of
empathy at all?* Table \@ref(tab:raw) gives the raw rates, adjusted so that
a thread's AI replies carry no more total weight than its real replies (see
"Making a fair comparison").

```{r raw}
raw_rates %>%
  mutate(across(c(ER, IP, EX), pct1)) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("", "Emotional reaction", "Interpretation", "Exploration"),
        align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
        caption = "Share of replies showing each kind of empathy (weighted).")
```

## The four moderators

A *moderator* is a variable that changes the size of an effect; here, the
real-vs-AI gap. We examined these four in the main analysis; the prompting strategy, a fifth
factor, is examined in Section \@ref(res-strat).

1. **Topic.** A language model read each opening post and assigned one of
   17 medical disciplines (taxonomy from Chan et al., 2025). The label belongs
   to the thread, so a reply to a skin question is a "dermatology" reply
   whether a clinician or an AI wrote it. We merged some related disciplines
   (cardiology with pulmonology, dentistry with otolaryngology, neurology with
   ophthalmology, haematology/immunology with infectious diseases) and left out
   the two catch-all labels ("Medical; other", "Nonmedical"), leaving
   `r n_topics` topics and `r fmt(n_threads_in)` threads (Table \@ref(tab:topics)).
   `r n_expl` topic (Neoplasms) is small (under 5% of threads); it stays in the
   analysis but is flagged as exploratory.
2. **Which AI model** wrote the reply: does a topic affect Gemini, OpenAI and
   Grok differently?
3. **Cancer relevance.** A language-model flag for threads where cancer is
   involved (`r fmt(n_cancer)` threads; `r n_cancer_na` threads without a flag
   are dropped from this analysis only).
4. **Severity.** A 1-4 triage score for how serious the patient's problem is,
   from a collaborator's rating of each post. `r fmt(n_sev_na)` threads have no
   usable score (almost all rated "not applicable"); we do not treat these as low
   severity but give them their own indicator.

```{r topics}
lookup %>%
  arrange(desc(n_threads)) %>%
  mutate(share = pct1(share), n_threads = fmt(n_threads),
         exploratory = ifelse(exploratory, "yes", "")) %>%
  select(topic_label, n_threads, share, exploratory) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Topic", "Threads", "Share of all threads", "Exploratory (< 5%)"),
        align = c("l", "r", "r", "c"),
        caption = "The topics used in the analysis.")
```

## Other variables we controlled for

A collaborator proposed several thread-level variables. All models adjust for
them: who the post is about (the poster or someone else), the patient's age and
sex where stated, severity, and whether the first responder's declared
specialty matches the topic of the post (real replies only, since the AI
has no specialty). Missing values are coded with their own indicator rather
than guessed. Because these variables belong to the thread, and each thread
already has its own baseline in the models, they can only change the real-vs-AI
gap if we ask them to; severity is the one we tested that way. For the others
we report the effects on how often replies show empathy at all
(Section \@ref(res-cov)).

## Making a fair comparison

- **Replies in a thread are not independent.** A frightening question may draw
  empathy from everyone. Each thread has its own baseline in the model
  (a random intercept), so the comparison of real and AI replies is made
  *within* threads.
- **AI models wrote more replies than there were real ones.** If a thread
  has 2 real replies and a model wrote 8, each of its 8 replies counts for
  1/4, so both sides carry equal weight. This uses all the data and avoids
  the arbitrariness of randomly discarding replies. Reported intervals are
  approximate under this scheme.

## How to read the numbers

- **Odds ratio (OR).** The odds of a reply showing empathy are
  P/(1-P). The *gap* is the AI-to-real ratio of these odds *within the same
  thread*: below 1 means AI is less likely to show empathy, 0.5 means half the
  odds, above 1 means more likely. Because the comparison is within threads,
  these ratios are more extreme than the raw percentages in
  Table \@ref(tab:raw) would suggest.
- **Shift.** How much a moderator multiplies the gap relative to its average.
  For a topic: shift 1.3 means the gap is 1.3 times the average gap in that
  topic. If the average gap is below 1, a shift above 1 therefore means the AI
  is *closer to* real replies than average there.
- **95% credible interval.** The range that holds the true value with 95%
  probability given the data and model (a Bayesian analogue of a confidence
  interval).
- **pd (probability of direction).** The posterior probability that the effect
  has the sign we report. It is not a p-value. We call a result **credible**
  when pd exceeds 0.975 *and* the interval excludes 1.
- **Partial pooling.** Topic effects are treated like random effects:
  topics with plenty of threads get mostly their own estimate, topics with few
  are pulled toward the average. This guards against over-reading small topics
  and is why we apply no separate multiple-comparison correction.

# What to keep in mind {#caveats}

- **Topic labels are noisy.** The labelling model agrees with a 200-post
  reference set about 77% of the time, and the reference was itself built
  largely by language models. Roughly one label in four may be off. Noise in a
  grouping variable blurs real differences, so a missing topic effect is weaker
  evidence than it looks, and detected ones are probably underestimates.
- **Topic comes from the post, not the reply.** A reply that wanders off topic
  keeps the post's label.
- **Many comparisons, partial protection.** We look at
  `r nrow(bt)` pooled topic shifts and `r nrow(btl)` model-specific ones. Pooling
  limits false alarms, but around one in forty estimates can look credible by
  chance. Treat individual topics as leads, not conclusions, especially the
  exploratory topic.
- **Strategies and topic.** The per-model topic shifts in Section \@ref(res-llm)
  are shared by a model's three prompting strategies. Whether topic effects
  differ by strategy is examined only through variance components
  (Section \@ref(res-strat)), not topic by topic.
- **Reply length.** Length strongly affects what the classifiers detect and is
  partly a consequence of the strategy. Gaps are shown with and without
  adjusting for it; neither is the single "correct" answer (Section \@ref(res-len)).
- **Classifiers, not people.** All results describe what the classifiers
  detect.
- **Severity and specialty match are observational covariates.** Severity is
  a rating of the post; specialty match is partly a choice by whoever answers.
  We report associations, not causes.
- **Subsampling check is a single draw.** Randomly thinning AI replies instead
  of weighting them gives the same picture (Section \@ref(res-sub)), but we ran
  one random thinning, so draw-to-draw variation is not quantified.

# Results {#results}

## Model checks

```{r conv-text}
model_names <- c(C2_topic_gap = "pooled topic model", D2_cancer = "cancer model",
                 E_topic_by_llm = "topic-by-model model", F_severity = "severity model")
bad <- conv[!conv$converged, ]
conv_msg <- if (nrow(bad) == 0) {
  sprintf("All %d fits met the convergence criteria (largest max Rhat %.4f, smallest effective-sample-size ratio %.3f, no divergent transitions).",
          nrow(conv), max(conv$max_rhat), min(conv$min_neff_ratio))
} else {
  sprintf("%d of %d fits met every convergence criterion. The exception%s: %s.",
          sum(conv$converged), nrow(conv), ifelse(nrow(bad) > 1, "s", ""),
          paste(vapply(seq_len(nrow(bad)), function(k) {
            r <- bad[k, ]
            sprintf("%s, %s (%s)", mech_names[[r$mechanism]], model_names[[r$model]],
                    paste(c(if (r$max_rhat >= 1.01) sprintf("max Rhat %.4f", r$max_rhat),
                            if (r$min_neff_ratio <= 0.1) sprintf("effective-sample-size ratio %.3f", r$min_neff_ratio),
                            if (isTRUE(r$divergent_transitions > 0)) sprintf("%d divergent transitions", r$divergent_transitions)),
                          collapse = ", "))
          }, character(1)), collapse = "; "))
}
```

`r conv_msg` Fits that initially fell short were rerun with twice as many
iterations (Methods); this did not change which effects are credible.

```{r conv-v3}
v3lab <- c(L0_nolength = "strategy model without length adjustment", L1_length = "strategy model with length adjustment",
           H_severity_by_group = "severity-by-group model", I_topic_by_group = "topic-by-model-and-strategy model",
           C2_no_topic_intercept = "IP sensitivity model without topic intercept")
conv_sentence <- function(cv, what) {
  bad <- cv[!cv$converged, ]
  if (nrow(bad) == 0) return(sprintf("All %d %s fits met the convergence criteria.", nrow(cv), what))
  sprintf("%d of %d %s fits met every convergence criterion. The exception%s: %s.",
          sum(cv$converged), nrow(cv), what, ifelse(nrow(bad) > 1, "s", ""),
          paste(vapply(seq_len(nrow(bad)), function(k) {
            r <- bad[k, ]
            sprintf("%s, %s (%s)", mech_names[[r$mechanism]], v3lab[[r$model]],
                    paste(c(if (r$max_rhat >= 1.01) sprintf("max Rhat %.4f", r$max_rhat),
                            if (r$min_neff_ratio <= 0.1) sprintf("effective-sample-size ratio %.3f", r$min_neff_ratio),
                            if (isTRUE(r$divergent_transitions > 0)) sprintf("%d divergent transition%s", r$divergent_transitions, ifelse(r$divergent_transitions == 1, "", "s"))),
                          collapse = ", "))
          }, character(1)), collapse = "; "))
}
v3_all <- bind_rows(v3conv, v3sens_conv)
v3_msg <- conv_sentence(v3_all, "prompting-strategy")
sub_msg <- conv_sentence(sub_conv, "subsampling-check")
```

`r v3_msg` The largest Rhat among them is `r sprintf("%.4f", max(v3_all$max_rhat))`
and the smallest effective-sample-size ratio `r sprintf("%.3f", min(v3_all$min_neff_ratio))`;
four fits that were marginal at 2,000 iterations were refitted with 4,000. The few
divergent transitions that remain are a handful out of 12,000 draws per fit, and Rhat
and effective sample size are fine for these fits; we report them with that caveat. The
key results for the affected fits (severity for interpretations, topic variation for
explorations) are reproduced in the independent subsampling check below. `r sub_msg` The shortfalls in the subsampling check
are marginal as well (max Rhat `r sprintf("%.4f", max(sub_conv$max_rhat))`).

## The average gap, and how much it varies by topic

Table \@ref(tab:sd) shows the average gap and how much it moves from topic to
topic. "Spread" is the standard deviation of the topic shifts on the log-odds
scale; a spread of 0.44 means a typical topic multiplies the gap by about
$e^{0.44} \approx 1.55$ (or divides it by that).

```{r sd}
sd_slope <- sdp %>% filter(parameter == "topic_slope_sd")
tab <- avg %>%
  transmute(mechanism, avg_gap = or3(gap_or, gap_lcl, gap_ucl)) %>%
  left_join(sd_slope %>% transmute(mechanism, spread = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f-%.2f)", median, lcl, ucl),
                                   factor = sprintf("x%.2f", exp(median))), by = "mechanism") %>%
  mutate(mechanism = mech_names[mechanism])
kable(tab, col.names = c("Empathy type", "Average gap, OR (95% CrI)",
                         "Spread across topics, SD (95% CrI)", "Typical factor"),
      align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
      caption = "Average real-vs-AI gap (all AI replies pooled) and its variation across topics.")
```

`r sprintf("The spread's lower bound is clearly above zero (above 0.05) for %d of %d kinds of empathy", sum(sd_slope$lcl > 0.05), nrow(sd_slope))`,
so topic does change the gap. The effect is largest for explorations. Figure
\@ref(fig:forest) shows each topic's gap; filled points are topics whose shift
from the average is credible.

```{r forest, fig.width=9, fig.height=6.5, fig.cap="Real-vs-AI gap by topic (odds ratio, log scale; below 1 = AI less likely to show empathy). Filled points: credible shift from the average. Starred: under 5% of threads (exploratory). Dashed line: no gap; dotted red line: average over topics."}
plot_df <- bt %>%
  mutate(mechanism = factor(mech_names[mechanism], levels = unname(mech_names)),
         label = paste0(topic_label, ifelse(exploratory, " *", "")),
         label = factor(label, levels = unique(label[order(n_threads)])))
avg_df <- avg %>% mutate(mechanism = factor(mech_names[mechanism], levels = unname(mech_names)))
ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = gap_or, y = label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(data = avg_df, aes(xintercept = gap_or), linetype = "dotted", colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = gap_lcl, xmax = gap_ucl), height = 0, colour = "grey55") +
  geom_point(aes(fill = credible), shape = 21, size = 2.6, colour = "black") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "black", `FALSE` = "white"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~mechanism, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Gap: odds ratio, AI vs. real (95% credible interval)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

`r sum(bt$credible)` of the `r nrow(bt)` topic shifts are credible
(Table \@ref(tab:credible)). For Emotional Reactions and Explorations the AI trails real replies in
every topic and the topic only changes by how much. For Interpretations the AI
is on par with or ahead of real replies in some topics (cardiopulmonary,
neurologic and visual, and musculoskeletal); in none of them does the
interval lie clearly above 1, with musculoskeletal the closest.

```{r credible}
cr <- bt %>% filter(credible) %>%
  arrange(match(mechanism, names(mech_names)), desc(n_threads)) %>%
  transmute(mechanism = mech_names[mechanism],
            topic = paste0(topic_label, ifelse(exploratory, " *", "")),
            threads = n_threads,
            gap = or3(gap_or, gap_lcl, gap_ucl),
            shift = or3(shift_or, shift_lcl, shift_ucl),
            pd = sprintf("%.3f", shift_pd),
            read = ifelse(shift_or > 1, "AI closer to real than average", "AI further from real than average"))
kable(cr, col.names = c("Empathy type", "Topic", "Threads", "Gap, OR (95% CrI)", "Shift, OR (95% CrI)", "pd", "Reading"),
      align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "l"),
      caption = "Topics whose gap credibly differs from the average (pooled AI replies).")
```

## Do the AI models differ in how topic matters? {#res-llm}

First, how big is each model's average gap (Table \@ref(tab:llmgap))? This is
the baseline the topic shifts are measured against.

```{r llmgap}
avg_llm %>%
  transmute(mechanism = mech_names[mechanism], model = who_n, gap = or3(gap_or, gap_lcl, gap_ucl)) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = gap) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Empathy type", "Gemini", "OpenAI", "Grok"), align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
        caption = "Average real-vs-AI gap per AI model, odds ratio (95% CrI).")
```

Second, does a topic shift the gap by a different amount for each model? If
the models responded to topics in the same way, their topic shifts would move
together. Table \@ref(tab:llmsd) gives the spread of topic shifts per model.

```{r llmsd}
sd_rows <- sdl %>% filter(grepl("^topic_slope_sd_", parameter)) %>%
  mutate(model = c(gem = "Gemini", opn = "OpenAI", grk = "Grok")[sub("topic_slope_sd_", "", parameter)],
         txt = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f-%.2f)", median, lcl, ucl)) %>%
  select(mechanism, model, txt) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = txt) %>%
  mutate(mechanism = mech_names[mechanism])
kable(sd_rows[, c("mechanism", "Gemini", "OpenAI", "Grok")],
      col.names = c("Empathy type", "Gemini", "OpenAI", "Grok"), align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
      caption = "Spread of the topic shifts per AI model, SD on the log-odds scale (95% CrI).")
```

Topic matters for each model for explorations (spread about 0.5 for all three),
and less consistently for the other two kinds. The topic shifts of the
different models are mostly positively related (estimated correlations from
-0.1 to 0.55), but with 11 topics these correlations are very uncertain (every
interval includes zero), so we cannot say how closely the models track one
another.

Figure \@ref(fig:llmforest) shows each model's shift by topic.
`r sum(btl$credible)` of `r nrow(btl)` shifts are credible
(Table \@ref(tab:llmcred)).

```{r llmforest, fig.width=9.5, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Topic shift of the real-vs-AI gap by AI model (odds ratio, log scale). Above 1: gap smaller than that model's average in that topic; below 1: larger. Filled: credible. Starred topic: exploratory."}
pl <- btl %>%
  mutate(mechanism = factor(mech_names[mechanism], levels = unname(mech_names)),
         label = paste0(topic_label, ifelse(exploratory, " *", "")),
         label = factor(label, levels = unique(label[order(n_threads)])),
         who_n = factor(who_n, levels = unname(llm_names)))
ggplot(pl, aes(x = shift_or, y = label, colour = who_n, shape = credible)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = shift_lcl, xmax = shift_ucl), orientation = "y",
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), size = 0.35, linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 16, `FALSE` = 1), guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = llm_cols, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~mechanism) +
  labs(x = "Shift in gap relative to the model's average (odds ratio, 95% CrI)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
        legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r llmcred}
crl <- btl %>% filter(credible) %>%
  arrange(match(mechanism, names(mech_names)), who_n, desc(n_threads)) %>%
  transmute(mechanism = mech_names[mechanism], model = who_n,
            topic = paste0(topic_label, ifelse(exploratory, " *", "")),
            gap = or3(gap_or, gap_lcl, gap_ucl), shift = or3(shift_or, shift_lcl, shift_ucl),
            pd = sprintf("%.3f", shift_pd))
kable(crl, col.names = c("Empathy type", "Model", "Topic", "Gap in topic, OR (95% CrI)", "Shift, OR (95% CrI)", "pd"),
      align = c("l", "l", "l", "r", "r", "r"),
      caption = "Model-specific topic shifts that are credible.")
```

Finally, do two models differ in how a topic affects them? We compared the
shifts of each pair of models in each topic (`r nrow(dl)` comparisons).
`r if (sum(dl$credible) == 0) "None is credible." else sprintf("%d %s credible:", sum(dl$credible), ifelse(sum(dl$credible) == 1, "is", "are"))`

```{r dcred, results='asis'}
dc <- dl %>% filter(credible) %>% arrange(match(mechanism, names(mech_names)))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(dc))) {
  r <- dc[i, ]
  cat(sprintf("- **%s, %s, %s%s:** shift ratio %s (pd %.3f).\n", mech_names[r$mechanism], r$pair, r$topic_label,
              ifelse(r$exploratory, " (exploratory topic)", ""),
              or3(r$shift_ratio_or, r$shift_ratio_lcl, r$shift_ratio_ucl), r$shift_ratio_pd))
}
```

A shift ratio above 1 means the first model gains more than the second in that
topic, relative to each model's own average. Such differences between models are
rare, so the topic effects are largely common to the models.

## Cancer-related threads

```{r cancer, results='asis'}
for (i in seq_len(nrow(canc))) {
  r <- canc[i, ]
  cred <- is_cred(r$shift_pd, r$shift_lcl, r$shift_ucl)
  cat(sprintf("- **%s:** gap %s in other threads, %s in cancer-related threads. %s\n",
              mech_names[r$mechanism], f1(r$gap_not_cancer_or),
              or3(r$gap_cancer_or, r$gap_cancer_lcl, r$gap_cancer_ucl),
              if (cred) sprintf("The gap is credibly %s in cancer-related threads (shift %s, pd %.3f), meaning the AI is relatively %s there.",
                                ifelse(r$shift_or > 1, "smaller", "larger"),
                                or3(r$shift_or, r$shift_lcl, r$shift_ucl), r$shift_pd,
                                ifelse(r$shift_or > 1, "better", "worse"))
              else sprintf("No credible difference (shift %s, pd %.3f).", or3(r$shift_or, r$shift_lcl, r$shift_ucl), r$shift_pd)))
}
```

The cancer flag is separate from the "Neoplasms" topic, which is smaller and
only includes posts where a clinician or test has raised the concern. A
borderline interval (one end near 1) is weak evidence.

## Severity {#res-sev}

If the real-vs-AI gap depends on how severe the problem is, a severity
effect on its own is not enough: it must differ between real and AI replies.
We tested this with an interaction between severity and being AI-written,
separately for each model. Each number in Table \@ref(tab:sev) is how
much the gap changes (multiplies) per additional severity level (the scale
runs 1-4). A value above 1 means AI replies catch up with real ones as severity
rises; below 1 means they fall further behind.

```{r sev}
sv <- sev_cred %>% filter(grepl("per severity", term)) %>%
  mutate(who = ifelse(who %in% names(llm_names), llm_names[who], "All AI (mean of the three)"),
         txt = paste0(or3(sev_or, sev_lcl, sev_ucl), ifelse(credible, " *", ""))) %>%
  select(mechanism, who, txt) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = mechanism, values_from = txt)
kable(sv[, c("who", "ER", "IP", "EX")],
      col.names = c("", mech_names[["ER"]], mech_names[["IP"]], mech_names[["EX"]]),
      align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
      caption = "Change in the real-vs-AI gap per severity level, factor (95% CrI). * = credible.")
```

For interpretations the gap shrinks with severity for all three models.
For emotional reactions this holds for Gemini and OpenAI but not Grok, and the
average over the three is borderline. For explorations severity does not
change the gap. Threads with no usable severity rating
(`r fmt(n_sev_na)` threads) differ strongly in their overall gap, but this
probably reflects what kind of post cannot be rated, so we do not interpret it.

## Prompting strategies {#res-strat}

Each AI model wrote its replies under three prompting strategies, DG, SAG and
SAGII. Sections above pool them. Here we ask three questions: do the
strategies differ in how far they fall short of real replies, does the
strategy change how severity matters, and does it change how topic matters?
We report strategy differences *within* each model, because a strategy can
work differently in different models. All gaps in this section adjust for
reply length unless stated otherwise (see next subsection for why).

### Reply length and the interpretation gap {#res-len}

How long a reply is matters a lot for what the classifiers detect. Each
doubling of length multiplies the odds of showing interpretation by about
`r f1(per_doubling("IP"))`, emotional reaction by `r f1(per_doubling("ER"))`, and
exploration by `r f1(per_doubling("EX"))` (shorter replies are more often flagged as
exploring). The AI models differ in length: the median real reply has
`r wmed("real")` words (mean `r round(wavg("real"))`, a long tail), against
`r wmed("gemini")` for Gemini, `r wmed("openai")` for OpenAI and `r wmed("grok")` for Grok.

Table \@ref(tab:lentab) puts three comparisons side by side. *Raw* compares the
shares in the first two columns directly. *Within thread, no length
adjustment* compares real and AI replies in the same thread, as everywhere in this report.
*Within thread, length adjusted* additionally compares replies of the same
length.

```{r lentab}
rl <- raw_rates %>% tidyr::pivot_longer(c(ER, IP, EX), names_to = "mechanism", values_to = "rate")
real_r <- rl %>% filter(who == "Real clinicians") %>% transmute(mechanism, real = rate)
lt <- rl %>% filter(who != "Real clinicians") %>%
  mutate(model = names(llm_names)[match(sub("AI: ", "", who), llm_names)]) %>%
  left_join(real_r, by = "mechanism") %>%
  mutate(raw_or = (rate / (1 - rate)) / (real / (1 - real))) %>%
  left_join(ge %>% filter(level == "model", spec == "no length adjustment") %>%
              transmute(mechanism, model = who, or0 = or3(or, lcl, ucl)), by = c("mechanism", "model")) %>%
  left_join(ge %>% filter(level == "model", spec == "length adjusted") %>%
              transmute(mechanism, model = who, or1 = or3(or, lcl, ucl)), by = c("mechanism", "model")) %>%
  arrange(match(mechanism, names(mech_names)), match(model, model_order)) %>%
  transmute(mechanism = mech_names[mechanism], model = llm_names[model], real = pct1(real), ai = pct1(rate),
            raw = f1(raw_or), or0, or1)
kable(lt, col.names = c("Empathy type", "AI model", "Real replies", "AI replies", "Raw odds ratio",
                        "Within thread, no length adjustment", "Within thread, length adjusted"),
      align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
      caption = "Real-vs-AI gap for each AI model: raw shares, within-thread gap, and within-thread gap adjusted for reply length (odds ratio, 95% CrI).")
```

For interpretations the adjustment changes the picture. OpenAI's replies are
long, and long replies are classified as interpretation more often, so without
the adjustment OpenAI appears to match or exceed real clinicians
(raw `r pct1(rl$rate[rl$who == "AI: OpenAI" & rl$mechanism == "IP"])` vs.
`r pct1(real_r$real[real_r$mechanism == "IP"])` for real replies; within-thread gap
`r gx_txt("no length adjustment", "model", "openai", "IP")`). At equal length it falls
behind (`r gx_txt("length adjusted", "model", "openai", "IP")`). For Gemini and Grok, whose
replies are about as long as the *typical* real reply but shorter than the real
average, the adjustment moves the other way: Gemini from
`r gx_txt("no length adjustment", "model", "gemini", "IP")` to
`r gx_txt("length adjusted", "model", "gemini", "IP")`, and Grok from
`r gx_txt("no length adjustment", "model", "grok", "IP")` to
`r gx_txt("length adjusted", "model", "grok", "IP")`. For emotional reactions the
adjustment matters moderately and for explorations hardly at all.

Which version to quote depends on the question. The unadjusted gap describes
the replies as they are; the adjusted gap asks whether an AI reply is as empathic *as a
real reply of the same length*. Since length is partly a result of the
prompting strategy, the adjusted gap is not simply "more correct". Everything
else in this section uses the adjusted version; the unadjusted one is in the
saved results (`v3_group_effects.csv`).

### Gap by model and strategy

Table \@ref(tab:grouptab) gives the gap for each of the nine model-by-strategy
groups, and for each model averaged over its three strategies.

```{r grouptab}
wide_groups <- function(spec_name, with_star) {
  d <- ge %>% filter(spec == spec_name, level %in% c("group", "model")) %>%
    mutate(model = sub("_.*$", "", who),
           strat = ifelse(level == "group", sub("^.*_", "", who), "mean"),
           txt = if (with_star) star(or3(or, lcl, ucl), credible) else or3(or, lcl, ucl)) %>%
    select(mechanism, model, strat, txt) %>%
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = mechanism, values_from = txt) %>%
    arrange(match(model, model_order), match(strat, c("dg", "sag", "sagii", "mean"))) %>%
    mutate(model = llm_names[model], strat = ifelse(strat == "mean", "Mean of three strategies", strat_names[strat]))
  d[, c("model", "strat", "ER", "IP", "EX")]
}
kable(wide_groups("length adjusted", FALSE),
      col.names = c("AI model", "Strategy", mech_names[["ER"]], mech_names[["IP"]], mech_names[["EX"]]),
      align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r"),
      caption = "Real-vs-AI gap (length adjusted) for each model-by-strategy group, odds ratio (95% CrI).")
```

```{r rangetxt}
rng <- function(mech, level) {
  d <- ge %>% filter(spec == "length adjusted", mechanism == mech, level == !!level)
  max(d$or) / min(d$or)
}
```

Differences between models are far larger than differences between
strategies. Averaged over strategies, the largest gap between two
models is a factor of `r f1(rng("ER", "model"))` for emotional reactions,
`r f1(rng("IP", "model"))` for interpretations and `r f1(rng("EX", "model"))`
for explorations; between strategies, averaged over models, it is only
`r f1(rng("ER", "strategy"))`, `r f1(rng("IP", "strategy"))` and
`r f1(rng("EX", "strategy"))`.

### Do strategies differ within a model?

Table \@ref(tab:contrasts) compares strategies directly. Each entry is the
ratio of the two strategies' gaps within the same model: a value below 1 for
"DG vs SAG" means DG falls further behind real replies than SAG does; above 1
means DG is closer to real. The last block averages over the three models.

```{r contrasts}
cw <- ge %>% filter(spec == "length adjusted", level %in% c("strategy_within_model", "strategy_across_models")) %>%
  mutate(who = ifelse(who == "all", "all", who),
         contrast = gsub("sagii", "SAGII", contrast),
         contrast = gsub("\\bsag\\b", "SAG", contrast),
         contrast = gsub("\\bdg\\b", "DG", contrast),
         contrast = gsub(" - ", " vs ", contrast),
         txt = star(or3(or, lcl, ucl), credible)) %>%
  select(mechanism, who, contrast, txt) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = mechanism, values_from = txt) %>%
  arrange(match(who, c(model_order, "all")), match(contrast, c("DG vs SAG", "DG vs SAGII", "SAG vs SAGII"))) %>%
  mutate(who = ifelse(who == "all", "All models (mean)", llm_names[who]))
kable(cw[, c("who", "contrast", "ER", "IP", "EX")],
      col.names = c("AI model", "Comparison", mech_names[["ER"]], mech_names[["IP"]], mech_names[["EX"]]),
      align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r"),
      caption = "Differences between prompting strategies in the real-vs-AI gap (length adjusted): ratio of gaps, odds ratio (95% CrI). * = credible.")
```

`r n_within_cred` of the `r n_within` within-model comparisons and
`r n_across_cred` of the `r n_across` pooled comparisons are credible. Three things stand out:

- **Emotional reactions:** DG is the weakest strategy on average
  (DG vs SAG `r gx_txt("length adjusted", "strategy_across_models", "all", "ER", "dg - sag")`,
  DG vs SAGII `r gx_txt("length adjusted", "strategy_across_models", "all", "ER", "dg - sagii")`).
  This is driven by OpenAI (DG vs SAG
  `r gx_txt("length adjusted", "strategy_within_model", "openai", "ER", "dg - sag")`) and by
  Grok, where SAG comes closest to real replies (DG vs SAG
  `r gx_txt("length adjusted", "strategy_within_model", "grok", "ER", "dg - sag")`; SAG vs SAGII
  `r gx_txt("length adjusted", "strategy_within_model", "grok", "ER", "sag - sagii")`).
- **Interpretations:** the pooled comparisons are close to 1; only SAG vs SAGII
  (`r gx_txt("length adjusted", "strategy_across_models", "all", "IP", "sag - sagii")`) is credible, and its
  interval ends at 1. Within models, the credible differences are small: Gemini SAG vs SAGII
  `r gx_txt("length adjusted", "strategy_within_model", "gemini", "IP", "sag - sagii")` and OpenAI DG vs SAG
  `r gx_txt("length adjusted", "strategy_within_model", "openai", "IP", "dg - sag")`.
- **Explorations:** no pooled difference. Within OpenAI the DG gap is about
  twice that of SAG (DG vs SAG
  `r gx_txt("length adjusted", "strategy_within_model", "openai", "EX", "dg - sag")`), i.e. DG is
  *closer* to real replies, but the explorations gaps of OpenAI and Grok are very large
  (odds roughly 30 to 40 times lower than real), so these ratios describe small differences between small rates.

Because the sign and size of strategy differences change from model to model,
"which strategy is best" has no model-independent answer. The evidence for the
borderline comparisons (pd just above or below 0.975) is not strong enough to
single any of them out (see Section \@ref(res-sub)).

### Does severity matter differently for each strategy?

Section \@ref(res-sev) tested whether the gap changes with severity, per model. Table
\@ref(tab:sevgroup) does so for each of the nine groups (extra change in the gap
per severity level; above 1 = the AI catches up as severity rises).

```{r sevgroup}
kable(wide_groups("severity by group", TRUE),
      col.names = c("AI model", "Strategy", mech_names[["ER"]], mech_names[["IP"]], mech_names[["EX"]]),
      align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r"),
      caption = "Change in the real-vs-AI gap per severity level, by model and strategy, factor (95% CrI). * = credible.")
sev_grp <- ge %>% filter(spec == "severity by group", level == "group")
sev_cmp_w <- ge %>% filter(spec == "severity by group", level %in% c("strategy_within_model", "strategy_across_models"))
```

For interpretations the severity effect is credible in `r sum(sev_grp$credible[sev_grp$mechanism == "IP"])` of 9 groups,
whichever strategy was used. For emotional reactions it is credible in
`r sum(sev_grp$credible[sev_grp$mechanism == "ER"])` of 9 groups and for explorations in
`r sum(sev_grp$credible[sev_grp$mechanism == "EX"])`. Strategies barely differ in how
severity matters: of the `r nrow(sev_cmp_w)` strategy comparisons of severity slopes (all three kinds of empathy,
within models and pooled), `r sum(sev_cmp_w$credible)` `r ifelse(sum(sev_cmp_w$credible) == 1, "is", "are")` credible. So the
severity result of Section \@ref(res-sev) holds for each prompting strategy, not
only on average.

### Does topic matter differently for each model or strategy?

Estimating a separate topic effect for each of the nine groups (plus their
correlations) is beyond what 11 topics can support (see Outlook). Instead we
let each topic's shift have extra variation by AI model, by strategy and by
model-strategy group, each with one shared spread (standard deviation).
A spread near zero means topic does not matter differently for different
models or strategies.

```{r sdstrat}
sd_names <- c("topic_slope_sd (common shift)" = "Topic shift shared by all groups (for reference)",
              topic_x_model_sd = "Extra variation by AI model",
              topic_x_strategy_sd = "Extra variation by prompting strategy",
              topic_x_model_x_strategy_sd = "Extra variation by model-strategy group")
sdt <- v3sd %>% filter(parameter %in% names(sd_names)) %>%
  mutate(txt = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f-%.2f)", median, lcl, ucl), parameter = sd_names[parameter]) %>%
  select(mechanism, parameter, txt) %>% tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = mechanism, values_from = txt) %>%
  arrange(match(parameter, unname(sd_names)))
kable(sdt[, c("parameter", "ER", "IP", "EX")],
      col.names = c("Source of variation in the topic shift", mech_names[["ER"]], mech_names[["IP"]], mech_names[["EX"]]),
      align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
      caption = "Spread (SD, log-odds scale) of topic shifts of the real-vs-AI gap and its variation by model and strategy (95% CrI).")
clear <- v3sd %>% filter(parameter %in% c("topic_x_model_sd", "topic_x_strategy_sd", "topic_x_model_x_strategy_sd"), lcl > 0.05)
```

Topic effects vary very little by prompting strategy or by model-strategy
combination (estimated spreads of 0.04 or less). By AI model the variation is small for
emotional reactions and interpretations but substantial for explorations
(`r sprintf("%.2f", v3sd$median[v3sd$mechanism == "EX" & v3sd$parameter == "topic_x_model_sd"])`,
interval clearly above zero), in line with the two credible model differences
for explorations found in Section \@ref(res-llm). Strategy therefore does not
change *how topic matters*, beyond what the model already does.

```{r devcred, results='asis'}
dv <- v3dev %>% filter(credible)
if (nrow(dv) == 0) {
  cat("No individual topic-by-model, topic-by-strategy or topic-by-group deviation is credible.\n")
} else {
  cat(sprintf("%d individual deviation%s %s credible:\n\n", nrow(dv), ifelse(nrow(dv) == 1, "", "s"), ifelse(nrow(dv) == 1, "is", "are")))
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(dv))) {
    r <- dv[i, ]
    who <- paste(c(if (!is.na(r$model)) llm_names[[r$model]], if (!is.na(r$strategy)) strat_names[[r$strategy]]), collapse = ", ")
    cat(sprintf("- **%s, %s, %s%s:** shift %s (pd %.3f).\n", mech_names[[r$mechanism]], r$topic_label, who,
                ifelse(r$exploratory, " (exploratory topic)", ""), or3(r$or, r$lcl, r$ucl), r$pd))
  }
}
```

### Interpretations without the topic intercept {#res-sens}

The pooled topic model for interpretations in v2 had a few divergent
transitions, probably because the *baseline* differences between topics
(the random topic intercept) are almost zero for interpretations. We refitted it
without that intercept, with a stricter sampler setting, as a check.

```{r sens}
ip_v2 <- bt %>% filter(mechanism == "IP") %>%
  transmute(topic, v2_txt = paste0(or3(shift_or, shift_lcl, shift_ucl), " (pd ", sprintf("%.3f", shift_pd), ")"), v2_cred = credible)
sn <- v3sens %>% left_join(ip_v2, by = "topic") %>%
  mutate(sens_txt = paste0(or3(or, lcl, ucl), " (pd ", sprintf("%.3f", pd), ")"), sens_cred = credible)
sn_show <- sn %>% filter(v2_cred | sens_cred) %>% arrange(desc(n_threads)) %>%
  transmute(topic = paste0(topic_label, ifelse(exploratory, " *", "")), v2 = star(v2_txt, v2_cred), sens = star(sens_txt, sens_cred))
kable(sn_show, col.names = c("Topic", "Pooled topic model, shift (v2)", "Without topic intercept, shift"),
      align = c("l", "r", "r"),
      caption = "Interpretations: topic shifts of the gap, with and without the random topic intercept. * = credible; shown if credible in either.")
```

`r if (setequal(sn$topic[sn$v2_cred], sn$topic[sn$sens_cred])) sprintf("The same %d topics are credible in both versions and the shifts are almost identical (largest difference %.0f%% on the odds-ratio scale).", sum(sn$v2_cred), 100 * (exp(max(abs(log(sn$or / sn$v2_shift_or)))) - 1)) else sprintf("%d topics are credible in both versions, %d in only one (see table); the shifts are otherwise close (largest difference %.0f%%).", sum(sn$v2_cred & sn$sens_cred), sum(xor(sn$v2_cred, sn$sens_cred)), 100 * (exp(max(abs(log(sn$or / sn$v2_shift_or)))) - 1))`
The divergences therefore did not distort the topic findings for interpretations.

## Other covariates {#res-cov}

Table \@ref(tab:cov) shows how the other thread characteristics relate to
whether replies (real and AI alike, except where noted) show empathy. These
effects apply to the baseline rate, not the gap. Age is per decade; severity
per level; each is relative to a reference level (first-person posts, female
patients, rated severity, undeclared specialty).

```{r cov}
cov_lab <- c(subjectthird_party = "Post is about someone else", subjectunknown = "Post subject unclear",
             age10 = "Age (per decade)", age_na = "Age not stated",
             sex3male = "Male (vs. female)", sex3unknown = "Sex not stated",
             sev_c = "Severity (per level)", sev_na = "Severity not rated",
             real_match = "Real reply: first responder's specialty matches topic",
             real_mismatch = "Real reply: first responder's specialty differs from topic")
cv <- covs %>% mutate(credible = is_cred(effect_pd, effect_lcl, effect_ucl),
                      txt = paste0(or3(effect_or, effect_lcl, effect_ucl), ifelse(credible, " *", "")),
                      term = cov_lab[term]) %>%
  select(term, mechanism, txt) %>% tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = mechanism, values_from = txt)
kable(cv[, c("term", "ER", "IP", "EX")],
      col.names = c("", mech_names[["ER"]], mech_names[["IP"]], mech_names[["EX"]]),
      align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
      caption = "Association of thread characteristics with showing empathy, odds ratio (95% CrI). * = credible.")
```

Briefly: more severe problems draw more empathy of all kinds from both real
and AI replies; posts about someone else draw more interpretation (OR about
2.4); the demographic variables have small effects
(a few reach credibility, such as age for interpretations). Real replies in threads
where the first responder declared a body-system specialty show less emotional
reaction and exploration than threads without a declared specialty,
whether or not the specialty matches the topic. This probably reflects how
specialists write, or who chooses to declare a specialty, rather than the
match itself.

## Robustness: thinning instead of weighting {#res-sub}

The main models use all AI replies and give each a weight so that a thread's
AI replies carry no more total weight than its real replies. A different way
to treat the surplus is to randomly discard AI replies: in every thread, model
and strategy, we kept as many AI replies as the thread has real replies
(at random; cells with fewer replies are kept whole) and gave every reply
weight 1. This leaves `r fmt(77603)` AI replies instead of `r fmt(n_synth)`. We then
refitted all strategy models (length-adjusted and unadjusted gaps, severity
by group, topic by model and strategy) on the thinned data and compared them with the weighted fits.

```{r subsum}
spec_lab <- c("length adjusted" = "gap, length adjusted", "no length adjustment" = "gap, no length adjustment",
              "severity by group" = "severity slope")
level_lab <- c(group = "per model-by-strategy group", model = "per AI model", strategy = "per strategy",
               strategy_within_model = "strategy contrasts within a model", strategy_across_models = "strategy contrasts, pooled over models")
sc <- sub_cmp %>%
  group_by(spec, level) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), cw = sum(cred_w), cs = sum(cred_s), flips = sum(cred_w != cred_s),
            chg = 100 * (exp(max(abs(lratio))) - 1), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(match(spec, names(spec_lab)), match(level, names(level_lab))) %>%
  transmute(what = paste0(spec_lab[spec], ", ", level_lab[level]), n, cw, cs, flips, chg = sprintf("%.0f%%", chg))
kable(sc, col.names = c("Quantity", "Estimates", "Credible, weighted", "Credible, thinned",
                        "Credibility differs", "Largest change in odds ratio"),
      align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
      caption = "Weighted vs. thinned fits: how many estimates are credible in each, and how much the odds ratios move.")
```

The estimates are almost the same: the median change in an odds ratio is
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (exp(median(abs(sub_cmp$lratio))) - 1))`, the largest
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (exp(max(abs(sub_cmp$lratio))) - 1))`, and the intervals have the same width
(median ratio of interval widths `r sprintf("%.2f", median((sub_cmp$width_s) / sub_cmp$width_w))`).
The effect of length, the severity effects and the model gaps all reproduce, and so does the
topic-by-model spread for explorations (`r sprintf("%.2f", v3sd$median[v3sd$mechanism == "EX" & v3sd$parameter == "topic_x_model_sd"])` weighted).
`r sub_flip_n` of the `r nrow(sub_cmp)` estimates differ in whether they are credible. All of them are
comparisons between prompting strategies, with pd values between 0.92 and 0.99 in both fits:

```{r subflips}
who_lab <- function(w) vapply(w, function(x) {
  if (x == "all") "All models" else if (x %in% names(llm_names)) llm_names[[x]]
  else if (x %in% names(strat_names)) strat_names[[x]]
  else { pr <- strsplit(x, "_")[[1]]; paste(llm_names[[pr[1]]], strat_names[[pr[2]]]) }
}, character(1))
con_lab <- function(x) { x <- gsub("sagii", "SAGII", x); x <- gsub("\\bsag\\b", "SAG", x); x <- gsub("\\bdg\\b", "DG", x); gsub(" - ", " vs ", x) }
fl <- sub_cmp %>% filter(cred_w != cred_s) %>%
  mutate(what = paste0(spec_lab[spec], ", ", level_lab[level]),
         who_c = trimws(paste(who_lab(who), con_lab(contrast))),
         w = paste0(or3(or_w, lcl_w, ucl_w), " (pd ", sprintf("%.3f", pd_w), ")"),
         t = paste0(or3(or_s, lcl_s, ucl_s), " (pd ", sprintf("%.3f", pd_s), ")")) %>%
  arrange(match(mechanism, names(mech_names))) %>%
  transmute(mechanism = mech_names[mechanism], what, who_c, w, t)
kable(fl, col.names = c("Empathy type", "Quantity", "Which", "Weighted", "Thinned"),
      align = c("l", "l", "l", "r", "r"),
      caption = "Estimates whose credibility status differs between the weighted and the thinned fits.")
```

Nine of the ten are credible in the thinned fit but not in the weighted one; one (OpenAI, DG vs SAGII
for explorations) is the reverse. We therefore treat strategy
comparisons near the threshold as inconclusive rather than as findings.

```{r subtop}
sub_top <- sub_top %>% left_join(lookup %>% select(topic, topic_label), by = "topic")
drop <- sub_top %>% filter(cred_w, !cred_s)
gain <- sub_top %>% filter(!cred_w, cred_s)
```

The topic findings are also stable. In the topic-by-model-and-strategy model,
the pooled topic shifts change by at most
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (exp(max(abs(log(sub_top$or_s / sub_top$or_w)))) - 1))`.
`r sum(sub_top$cred_w)` shifts are credible with weighting and
`r sum(sub_top$cred_s)` after thinning;
`r if (nrow(drop) + nrow(gain) == 0) "none changes status." else paste0("the ones that lose credibility are ", paste(sprintf("%s, %s (shift %s to %s, pd %.3f to %.3f)", mech_names[drop$mech], drop$topic_label, f1(drop$or_w), f1(drop$or_s), drop$pd_w, drop$pd_s), collapse = "; "), ".")`
Weighting and thinning therefore give the same picture, which supports the choice
not to discard any replies. This is a single random thinning; repeating it would
show how much results vary between thinnings.

# Methods {#methods}

## Data and outcomes

All `r fmt(n_real + n_synth)` rated replies from `r fmt(n_threads)` threads
are used, with no outlier exclusion and no subsampling (a subsampling
sensitivity check is described below). Synthetic replies come
from Gemini, OpenAI and Grok, each under three prompting strategies (DG, SAG,
SAGII), giving nine synthetic groups plus the real group. Empathy labels
(0/1/2) for ER, IP and EX come from three fine-tuned RoBERTa bi-encoder
classifiers following EPITOME. The binary outcome is `label >= 1`. For IP and
EX label 1 never occurs in these data, so this equals `label == 2`.

## Topics and covariates

Topic labels come from the collaborators' pipeline (`classify_topics.py`):
gemini-2.5-pro at temperature 0, one of 17 disciplines per opening post,
joined on `submission_id`. Production-model agreement with a 200-post reference
sample was 0.770 (agreement between the two LLM annotators who built it:
0.795, $\kappa$ = 0.779). Four merges: Pulmonology + Cardiovascular,
Dentistry + Otolaryngology, Ophthalmology + Neurology, Hematology and immunology
+ Infectious diseases. "Nonmedical" and "Medical; other" are excluded from the
topic models. Topics under 5% of all threads are flagged exploratory but kept.

Covariates (all thread-level): `subject` (first person / third party /
unknown); `age10` (age in decades, centred at the median; missing set to 0 with
indicator `age_na`); `sex3` (female / male / unknown); `sev_c` (severity 1-4,
centred at the mean; "not applicable" and blank set to 0 with indicator
`sev_na`); `real_match` and `real_mismatch` (1 for real replies when the first
responder declared a body-system specialty that matches / does not match the
merged topic, else 0; reference: no declared body-system specialty; 0 for all
synthetic replies). Not used: weight, height, BMI, race, smoking, drinking and
time to first response, following the collaborator's documentation (heavy or
topic-dependent missingness).

## Response weights

With $n_c$ synthetic replies in a (thread, model, method) cell and $r$ real
replies in the thread, real replies have weight 1 and synthetic ones
$w = \min(1, r / n_c)$. Weights are computed on all threads before topic
filtering. In the subsampling check (Section \@ref(res-sub)), each such cell with
$n_c>r$ synthetic replies is instead thinned to $r$ randomly chosen replies
(seed 1, one draw), all weights are 1, and everything else is unchanged. They enter the log-likelihood as multipliers (`brms`
`weights()`), so estimates target the average over random per-thread
subsampling but posterior intervals are approximate.

## Models

Fitted separately for ER, IP and EX; Bernoulli likelihood, logit link. For
reply $i$: $s_i$ indicates a synthetic reply, $s_{iL}$ a reply from model $L$
(Gemini, OpenAI, Grok), $\beta_{g(i)}$ the coefficient for its group,
$\mathbf{x}_i$ the covariates above, $\ell_i$ log reply length in words,
$t(i)$ its thread's topic and $p(i)$ the thread.

**C2 (pooled topic moderation).**
$$\operatorname{logit} P(y_i=1)=\alpha+\beta_{g(i)}+\mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\delta+\gamma\ell_i+u_{t(i)}+v_{t(i)}s_i+a_{p(i)}$$
with $(u_t,v_t)\sim\mathcal N(0,\Sigma)$, $a_p\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_p^2)$. A
topic's gap is the mean of the nine synthetic $\beta_g$ plus $v_t$ (the shift),
exponentiated.

**E (topic moderation per model).** Replace $v_{t}s_i$ by
$\sum_L v_{tL}s_{iL}$, with $(u_t,v_{t,\mathrm{gem}},v_{t,\mathrm{opn}},v_{t,\mathrm{grk}})\sim\mathcal N(0,\Sigma)$
and an LKJ(2) prior on the correlations. A model's gap in a topic is the mean of
its three $\beta_g$ plus $v_{tL}$. Differences between models are computed from
the draws (ratio of gap ORs, ratio of shift ORs).

**D2 (cancer).** No topic effects;
$\ldots+\eta c_{p(i)}+\theta s_ic_{p(i)}+\ldots$ with cancer flag $c$; $\theta$ is the moderation.

**F (severity).** Model C2 plus $\sum_L\lambda_L s_{iL}\,\mathrm{sev}_i+\kappa s_i\,\mathrm{sevNA}_i$. Since
severity is also a covariate, $\lambda_L$ is the *extra* change in model $L$'s gap per
severity level, over and above any effect of severity on real replies;
the pooled value is the mean of the three. Topic effects stay in the model so
severity does not stand in for topic.

**L0 and L1 (strategy main effects).** Let $\beta_g$ be the coefficient of one of the nine
synthetic groups $g$ (model-by-strategy), real replies being the reference:
$$\operatorname{logit} P(y_i=1)=\alpha+\beta_{g(i)}+\mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\delta\,[+\gamma\ell_i]+a_{p(i)}.$$
L0 omits the length term, L1 includes it. A group's gap is $e^{\beta_g}$; a model's
gap is the exponentiated mean of its three $\beta_g$; a strategy's gap the mean over the
three models; strategy contrasts are differences of these quantities, computed from the draws.

**H (severity per group).** Model C2 with the length term, plus $\sum_g\lambda_g\,\mathbb 1[g(i)=g]\,\mathrm{sev}_i+\kappa s_i\,\mathrm{sevNA}_i$,
nine severity slopes instead of three. Slopes are summarised like the gaps above.

**I (topic by model and strategy).** Model C2 with the length term, plus extra topic
shifts $w_{t,L(i)}s_i+z_{t,m(i)}s_i+q_{t,g(i)}s_i$ by topic and AI model, topic and strategy,
and topic and group, with $w_{tL}\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_{TL}^2)$, $z_{tm}\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_{TM}^2)$,
$q_{tg}\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_{TG}^2)$ (one shared SD each; Normal(0, 1) prior truncated at 0). Real
replies have a dummy level with no data. The SDs say how much topic moderation varies by model, strategy
and group; individual deviations are reported but not interpreted as findings unless credible.

**Sensitivity for IP.** C2 with length adjustment, without the random topic intercept
$u_t$, `adapt_delta` = 0.99.

## Priors, sampling, convergence

Fixed effects: Normal(0, 2.5). Intercept and thread SD: Student-$t$(3, 0, 2.5).
Topic SDs: Normal(0, 1), truncated at 0. `brms` with `cmdstanr`; 4 chains of
2,000 iterations (1,000 warmup), 4 threads per chain, `adapt_delta` = 0.95,
seed 20260101. A fit is accepted when max $\hat R<1.01$, minimum
effective-sample-size ratio $>0.1$ and there are no divergent transitions.
Seven fits that fell marginally short (cancer models for all three kinds
of empathy, severity models for ER and EX, pooled topic models for IP and EX)
were refitted with 4,000 iterations (1,000 warmup); the credible topic effects
were unchanged. The refit of the IP pooled topic model improved
$\hat R$ but still has divergent transitions (reported under Model checks),
as in our earlier topic analysis; the topic-level intercept SD for
interpretations is close to zero, which makes the sampler's job harder. The strategy fits (L0, L1, H, I and the IP sensitivity fit) and the subsampling-check
fits use the same settings; four strategy fits that were marginal at 2,000 iterations
(IP and EX severity-by-group, EX topic-by-group, IP sensitivity) were refitted with 4,000.
Multithreaded summation makes draws non-reproducible from the seed
alone, so the saved fits (`models_bayesian/`) and the run metadata are the
reproducible artefacts.

## Reporting

Posterior median odds ratio, 95% highest-density interval and
$pd=\max\{P(\theta>0),P(\theta<0)\}$ on the log-odds scale. Credible: pd > 0.975
and the interval excludes 1. No frequentist multiplicity correction; topic
effects are partially pooled instead. Code: `3i_topic_llm_moderation_v2.R` (topic, model, severity, cancer),
`3j_strategy_models.R` (prompting strategies, length adjustment, IP sensitivity and, with
`SUBS_SEED`, the subsampling check) and `3k_subsampling_*.R` (comparison of weighted
and thinned fits).

## Limitations

- Misclassified topics attenuate moderation estimates; no correction applied.
- Topic effects by strategy and by model-strategy group are summarised by variance
  components only; individual deviations are noisy and mostly not credible.
- Length-adjusted gaps compare replies of the same length; since length is
  partly caused by the strategy, they complement rather than replace the unadjusted gaps.
- The subsampling check is one random draw; six of its twelve fits narrowly missed the
  convergence rule (Model checks).
- With 11 topics, correlations between models' topic shifts are poorly
  determined, and topic-specific cells for single models are noisy.
- The cancer flag is a distinct construct from the Neoplasms topic.
- Specialty match and severity are observational; severity not-rated threads
  have a different gap, which we do not interpret.
- Weighted intervals are approximate.

# Outlook: what we did not do {#outlook}

- **The full topic-by-strategy-by-model model.** A separate topic shift for each
  of the nine groups with their correlations is not impossible to run, but the
  data cannot support it: it needs 55 covariance parameters from 11 topics, cells
  are sparse (for example about 2% of Grok's replies show exploration), and it would
  produce around 300 topic-by-group estimates per kind of empathy. The variance
  components in Section \@ref(res-strat) are the estimable version of the
  question and say that, beyond the model, strategy hardly changes how topic matters.
- **Topic by severity.** Whether severity matters differently in different topics
  was not tested.
- **More than one thinning.** The subsampling check used one random draw.
- **Cleaner topic labels.** About one topic label in four may be wrong. A human-coded
  validation set would quantify how much this blurs the topic results.
